disputed_claims.claim: Consolidated theory's framing that the root cause is simply 'multiple independent OS processes' opening uncoordinated handles, implying the fix is purely topology/operational.
disputed_claims.dispute: Own code reading (hermes_state_registry.py, cron/scheduler.py, gateway/run.py, tui_gateway/methods_profiles.py) plus A01/A04 show this is imprecise in a way that matters for remediation. cron/scheduler.py IS registry-routed (acquire()/release_or_close() in _open_cron_session_db/_finalize_cron_session, A01-verified) so cron's contribution is a working-as-designed refcount-to-zero rotation, not a bug an operator can dial away without a code/holding-pattern change. tui_gateway's roster-poll opens a bare, unregistered SessionDB(read_only=True) specifically to avoid stalling on the registry's writable-handle wait; read-only handles do not themselves rotate the WAL via close, so roster-poll is a registry-bypass but a red herring as a rotation TRIGGER, weakening one leg of the original five-source framing. The two concretely reproducible, code-level defects are: (1) cli.py:2838's long-lived interactive-session bare SessionDB() (unresolved db_path, never registered) plus delegate_tool.py child handles that DO route through acquire() against the SAME physical file/inode but cannot dedupe against the parent -- a genuine second concurrent writer object on one file (independently reproduced by A01); and (2) the write-time guard's (_wal_generation_was_lost/_halt_if_db_generation_changed) total blindness to same-process siblings versus the open-time guard's explicit self-PID exemption (L01, confirmed by A04 and independently here).

disputed_claims.claim: L01's proposed write-time-guard fix (silently adopt the new generation when a same-process sibling is detected via _PathReadBudget) is a low-risk, near-final fix.
disputed_claims.dispute: Agree with A04's rebuttal: mere co-presence of a same-process sibling on the same path is not proof that sibling caused the rotation, and even with correct attribution, updating stat-identity bookkeeping without reopening the underlying sqlite3.Connection risks routing further commits into an orphaned, never-checkpointed WAL -- silent data loss, strictly worse than today's loud failure. This requires positive attribution (a monotonic per-path generation token) plus a correctness-sensitive in-place reconnect; it is code_fix_substantial for that sub-fix, not a quick patch.

disputed_claims.claim: consolidated.md's minority note that L12's orphan PID 1146711 was 'never identified' and is the single most concrete unexplained data point.
disputed_claims.dispute: Superseded by A02: system_watch.log's contemporaneous ps-aux snapshots (07:51/07:54/07:57) show PID 1146711 alive as 'python -m hermes_cli.main serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 0', started 07:48:2x alongside the Electron desktop process tree, exited by the 07:59:17 halt. This is the Hermes Desktop app's locally-spawned backend server -- a legitimate, already-named class of writer (ad-hoc/manually-launched process against the default state.db, registry-bypassing) not a mysterious sixth source. L12's 'unaccounted orphan' framing reflected an incomplete evidence sweep (post-hoc ps -ef after the process had exited), not a genuine gap in the writer-population enumeration.

confirmed_claims: The registry's handle-dedup (hermes_state_registry.py's _generations dict + threading.Lock) is process-local only; nothing in the module implements or references a cross-process primitive (flock, shared memory, socket) -- verified directly by reading the file's full acquire()/release()/_Generation logic.

hermes_state.py's close() performs a PASSIVE (not TRUNCATE) WAL checkpoint on a clean, non-generation-lost writable close, and an in-code comment explicitly names cron's per-job open+close cycle as the reason TRUNCATE was avoided at close time -- cron-driven WAL churn is a known, already-partially-mitigated concern in the code itself, not a novel discovery.

_wal_generation_was_lost()/_halt_if_db_generation_changed() (hermes_state.py) is a pure filesystem-identity (stat-based, with /proc fallback) check with zero process/PID/same-process-sibling awareness on the write-time path, confirming the open-time-vs-write-time asymmetry (L01, A04).

cli.py:2838 constructs an unregistered, unresolved-path SessionDB() for the whole interactive session, and delegate_tool.py's child-session opener resolves through hermes_state_registry.acquire() against the same physical file -- producing two concurrently live writer objects on one inode whenever a bare-SessionDB CLI session delegates to a subagent tool. This is the single most concretely reproducible double-writer vector in the swarm's findings (A01 independent re-verification).

tui_gateway's roster-poll opens SessionDB(read_only=True) directly, bypassing the registry, specifically to avoid stalling on the registry's writable-handle wait -- a real registry-bypass but read-only, so not itself a plausible generation-rotation trigger; the theory's framing of it as a contributing 'writer' overstates its role.

PID 1146711 (L12's orphan) is resolved by A02 via system_watch.log as the Hermes Desktop app's locally-spawned `hermes_cli.main serve` backend process, a legitimate but registry-bypassing writer consistent with the existing 'ad-hoc invocation' category -- not an unidentified sixth mechanism.

The guard's fail-closed, manual-restart-required behavior (DeletedWalGenerationError) is intentional and well-justified (L16, confidence 0.98): it stops a second opener from checkpointing/committing against a WAL generation this handle no longer shares, preventing the wrong-page/split-brain corruption class (#105670). No lane and no independent reading found this behavior itself to be a bug; it must not be weakened or auto-recovered.
missing_gap: No lane, including this one, tested empirically whether cron's parallel ThreadPoolExecutor (scheduler.py:508-977, found by A01) meaningfully reduces realized WAL-rotation frequency during overlapping job windows versus the 'many times/hour' framing -- a quantification gap that doesn't overturn the theory but is untested. Separately, once PID 1146711 is folded in as a resolved desktop-app instance (A02), the writer population is now fully enumerated among named categories (gateway, dashboard, cron-per-job, CLI/delegate_tool, ad-hoc desktop-spawned serve, tui roster-poll [read-only, non-triggering]) with no remaining unattributed data points across A01-A04 and this review.
verdict: The swarm's converged multi-writer theory is directionally correct and, after A01/A02/A04 and this independent code review, fully accounted for: no remaining unattributed writer processes (A02 resolves L12's orphan as a legitimate desktop-app-spawned serve process), and the mechanism (process-local-only registry dedup + a write-time guard blind to same-process siblings) is verified at the line level. The theory nonetheless overstates raw process COUNT as the driver and understates two more precise, more actionable facts: (a) cron's contribution is a working-as-designed, already-partially-mitigated pattern (registry-routed, PASSIVE-checkpoint-on-close), not a bug to fix operationally; (b) the two genuinely code-level defects are the CLI's unregistered long-lived handle racing its own delegate_tool children on one inode, and the write-time guard's PID-blind asymmetry versus the open-time guard's PID-aware exemption. tui_gateway roster-poll is a real registry-bypass but not a plausible rotation trigger (read-only), which is a minor correction to the theory's enumeration, not a refutation. A04's caution that any write-time-guard 'adopt' fix requires positive attribution (a monotonic generation token) and an in-place connection reopen -- not mere co-presence checking -- is correct and should gate any change to the guard itself.
final_root_cause_statement: DeletedWalGenerationError recurs because Hermes's writer-handle registry (hermes_state_registry.py) deduplicates SessionDB handles only within a single process and has no cross-process concept of the default state.db's current WAL generation, so whenever any writer's handle cleanly closes -- a cron job finishing its intentional, registry-routed per-job acquire/release cycle, an ad-hoc CLI one-shot or manually-launched desktop-app `hermes serve` instance being garbage-collected, or (most concretely and reproducibly) the interactive CLI's own long-lived-but-UNREGISTERED bare SessionDB() (cli.py:2838) racing its delegate_tool child handles, which DO route through the registry against the identical inode and therefore cannot be deduplicated against the parent -- SQLite's own close-time behavior unlinks/rotates the -wal/-shm sidecar files out from under any OTHER still-open long-lived handle (gateway, dashboard, or a sibling CLI/delegate handle); the write-time guard (_wal_generation_was_lost/_halt_if_db_generation_changed) then correctly and intentionally halts with a loud, manual-restart-required error specifically because it is a pure filesystem-identity check with no same-process-sibling awareness (unlike the open-time guard's explicit self-PID exemption), preventing a real split-brain/wrong-page corruption class rather than because the guard or its fail-closed philosophy is itself defective. tui_gateway's roster-poll is a real registry-bypass but is read-only and therefore not itself a rotation trigger, and L12's previously 'unidentified' orphan writer is resolved (A02) as a legitimate desktop-app-spawned serve process, so the incident's writer population is now fully enumerated with no remaining unexplained data points.
